correctness.rationale: For vertical phase U in (0,1), the sole integer layer is at height 1; its section is a square of side L=nU. The deterministic horizontal apex-dependent shifts preserve the independent uniform phases modulo one conditional on U. The two interval counts are independently floor(L)+Bernoulli(frac(L)). Write L=j+r; j is uniform on 0,...,n-1 and r independently uniform on [0,1). The probabilities of zero, one and two additional interval points, integrated over r, are each 1/3. Products are j^2, j(j+1), (j+1)^2; the first two coincide at j=0 and consecutive bins share the interior squares, with no further collisions. This includes n=1 and applies to every real apex displacement. Conditional mean is L^2; conditional second moment is [j^2+(2j+1)r]^2. Integrating and summing gives E N=n^2/3 and E N^2=n^4/5+n^2/9+1/45, hence the claimed variance. Each interval count is at distance at most 1 from nU; the product bound |N/n^2-U^2|<=2/n+1/n^2 establishes almost-sure convergence under common phases and the asserted CDF; the variance formula gives the coefficient of variation. Boundary events have translation measure zero, including over countably many n. The inspected rational checker compares finite section counts and finite moment sums only and was not executed.

Tokmachev's explicit independent-uniform formula applies to primitive integer triangles. The relevant square slices here have generally noninteger side length and are not triangles; splitting them into triangles would not make their counts independent.
The indexed simplex-frustum theorem specializes to simplex horizontal sections, not arbitrary bases.

value.rationale: A square pyramid with one lattice unit of height is a canonical convex polytope for isolating anisotropic count fluctuations as volumes diverge. The complete positive mass spectrum, including apex invariance and how interior and endpoint weights differ, gives an exact benchmark that generic mean-as-volume or fluctuation estimates miss. The nonzero limiting coefficient of variation quantifies why fixed-height growth is different from isotropic dilation; it is not itself a new general concentration principle.
